title: Madagascar’s Giant Bats Are Getting Smaller
paragraphs: Madagascar’s flying foxes, which are counted among the largest bats on Earth, appear to have shrunk in recent decades, according to a study by scientists at the Field Museum in Chicago, published in the Journal of Mammalogy. The idea began when one of the researchers noticed that bats stored in museum drawers looked noticeably larger than the animals she handled in the field.

The team measured twelve features of the skulls and teeth of 121 specimens held in nine museums, some collected more than 150 years ago. Skulls from before the 1980s averaged 3.6 millimetres, or about 6 percent, longer than later ones. That timing coincides with the moment when hunting shifted from small-scale subsistence to a commercial trade in markets and restaurants. Lead author Emily Cornelius Ruhs suggested a possible mechanism: “If you’re the biggest bat in the sky, you might be the easiest target.” The population has reportedly fallen from roughly 300,000 in the early 2000s by about two-thirds.

The conclusions should be read with caution. The study shows a correlation in time rather than direct proof, and habitat loss and climate change may contribute as well. Moreover, a smaller body size does not by itself show that the species is in danger. Genetic work on today’s bats could reveal how well the surviving populations are coping.

questions.q: What made the researchers start the study?
questions.a: Museum bats looked larger than bats caught in the field.

questions.q: What did hunting change around the 1980s?
questions.a: It moved from small-scale hunting to a commercial trade.

questions.q: Why is the evidence not conclusive?
questions.a: It shows a correlation in time, and other factors such as habitat loss may play a part.
